As of 500 PM Thursday...

KEY MESSAGE 1... An axis of showers storms will progress slowly 
ssewd across central NC through early Friday, with an associated 
risk of excessive rain mainly south of US-64.

The synoptic cold front has now mostly cleared our region and is 
draped near the SC/NC border. While rich Gulf moisture from Tropical 
Storm Bertha continues to funnel NE along and north of the front, 
with PW values of 2-2.4 inches across central NC, much of the 
precipitation is now on the cool/stable side of the boundary where 
surface winds are from the NE and dew points are dropping into the 
60s. SPC mesoanalysis depicts marginal SBCAPE of 500-1000 J/kg 
across the southern Piedmont, Sandhills, and central/southern 
Coastal Plain, with plenty of CIN as well. So rainfall rates have 
come down significantly from where they were this morning, and this 
relative lull in precipitation is expected to continue through the 
early evening. North of there in the stable regime, only some patchy 
light rain and drizzle will continue. Temperatures have 
underperformed guidance due to the widespread cloud cover and 
precipitation, generally ranging from the upper-60s to mid-70s. The 
current high of 73F at GSO would tie the record low maximum 
temperature for the date if it holds, while the current high of 74F 
at RDU would break the daily record low maximum of 76F.

Late this evening and overnight, high-res guidance depicts the 
boundary may lift slightly back north again, with another wave of 
convection riding along it. However, given the front should still be 
pretty far south, weaker instability compared to this morning should 
limit rainfall rates somewhat for most of the region. There could be 
still be some heavy rates across the southern Piedmont, Sandhills, 
and central/southern Coastal Plain, where a Flood Watch is in effect 
until 9 AM Friday. But the sandy soils and little rainfall that had 
fallen in those areas before this afternoon have kept FFG relatively 
high, and 12z HREF probabilities of exceeding FFG are less in the 
south tonight than they were this morning across the north. Thus WPC 
dropped the moderate (level 3 of 4) risk of excessive rainfall and 
now has a slight (level 2 of 4) risk across most of the area. 
Additional QPF from WPC through Friday morning is in the 1-2 inch 
range on average across this region, but locally higher amounts will 
be possible. 12z HREF LPMM depicts potential for very local amounts 
as high as 4-6+ inches, which would certainly be enough to cause 
issues if it falls in an urban area like Fayetteville or where heavy 
rain already fell today. No mainstem rivers are forecast to reach 
minor flood stage at this time, but it can't be ruled out along the 
Neuse, particularly at Smithfield where the current forecast reaches 
just below flood stage on Friday morning.


KEY MESSAGE 2... The slow moving cold front pivoting back NW may 
result in another heavy rain threat on Friday night, especially in 
southeastern parts of the area.

The cold front will remain pinned near the southern NC coast during 
the day on Friday, which should help a relative lull in 
precipitation occur across central NC during the afternoon and 
evening. As surface high pressure wedges into the Piedmont, cool NE 
flow will prevail in a CAD regime, with widespread stability and 
mainly places again not getting out of the 70s. Patchy light rain 
and drizzle will be possible as well.

A shortwave trough and associated surface low tracking to our south 
and east look to provide additional forcing for ascent on Friday 
night and help the boundary pivot back NW again into our region. 
Moisture will return with 70s surface dew points creeping back in 
and PW values increasing to 2-2.5 inches. How far NW the boundary is 
able to get is still uncertain, but the 12z HREF depicts increasing 
probabilities of exceeding FFG once again on Friday night, with 
localized LPMM totals as high as 1-3 inches. Given all the rain that 
will have already fallen up to that point, flooding may be a renewed 
concern, and WPC has the SE half of our area in a slight (level 2 of 
4) risk for excessive rainfall.


KEY MESSAGE 3... After another cool and rainy day Saturday, the 
chance of rain will decrease and temperatures will return to normal 
late July values.

The stationary front should remain somewhere along the North 
Carolina/South Carolina border on Saturday, keeping a chance for 
showers across the entire area, with the highest chances in the 
south. As the front continues to weaken, just an isolated 
thunderstorm will be possible on Sunday, and Monday appears to be 
the first widespread day of dry weather in several days. As low 
pressure moves along the US/Canadian border during the beginning of 
next week, the accompanying cold front could make it as far south as 
the Carolinas, bringing another chance for showers and storms.
